claim: BUB-1 is destabilized in the bub-3(ok3437) deletion mutant with overall protein levels down to below 25% of the levels in control worms
source: As previously shown, BUB-1 is destabilized in this mutant with its overall protein levels down to below 25% of the levels in control worms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) Kim et al., 2015.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited reference Kim et al., 2015

claim: BUB-1 at meiotic kinetochores is reduced by 57% on average in the bub-3 deletion mutant compared to controls
source: Accordingly, BUB-1 was also significantly reduced at meiotic kinetochores in this mutant, albeit to a much lower extent (57% reduction on average compared to controls) than the overall protein level reduction (Figure 1B).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B

claim: BUB-1 can be recruited at kinetochores independently of BUB-3 in C. elegans oocytes
source: This surprisingly suggested that, in contrast to in yeasts or mammalian cells, BUB-1 can be recruited at kinetochores independently of BUB-3 in C. elegans oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BUB-1 is still present at kinetochores in bub-3 deletion mutants, contrasting with findings in other organisms

claim: HCP-1 is reduced by 36% at meiotic kinetochores in the bub-3 deletion mutant
source: Importantly, the reduced BUB-1 kinetochore level in the bub-3 deletion mutant, correlated with significant reductions of HCP-1 (36% reduction) and CLS-2 (58% reduction) at meiotic kinetochores (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: CLS-2 is reduced by 58% at meiotic kinetochores in the bub-3 deletion mutant
source: Importantly, the reduced BUB-1 kinetochore level in the bub-3 deletion mutant, correlated with significant reductions of HCP-1 (36% reduction) and CLS-2 (58% reduction) at meiotic kinetochores (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: The BHC module can be recruited independently of BUB-3 to kinetochores in C. elegans oocytes
source: This suggests that in C. elegans oocytes the BHC module can be recruited independently of BUB-3 to kinetochores.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that reduced but functional BHC pools are present at kinetochores in bub-3 deletion mutants

claim: BUB-1 fails to localize to kinetochores in the presence of KNL-1∆85-505 after depletion of endogenous KNL-1
source: In contrast in the presence of KNL-1∆85-505, BUB-1 failed to localize to kinetochores (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1D

claim: GFP-tagged HCP-1 does not localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes
source: GFP-tagged HCP-1 and CLS-2 also did not localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 1E

claim: CLS-2 does not localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes
source: GFP-tagged HCP-1 and CLS-2 also did not localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 1F

claim: Kinetochore localization of BUB-1 depends on the KNL-1 MELT repeats
source: Thus kinetochore, but not ring-domain, localization of BUB-1 depends on the KNL-1 MELT repeats.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing BUB-1 fails to localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant

claim: BUB-1 ring domain localization requires the E3 SUMO-protein ligase GEI-17
source: In line with a previous study, we also confirmed that BUB-1 ring domain localization required the E3 SUMO-protein ligase GEI-17, and thus probably BUB-1 sumoylation (Figure 1H; Pelisch et al., 2017).
evidence: Confirmed by imaging in Figure 1H and supported by citation to Pelisch et al., 2017

claim: BUB-1 ring domain localization probably requires BUB-1 sumoylation
source: In line with a previous study, we also confirmed that BUB-1 ring domain localization required the E3 SUMO-protein ligase GEI-17, and thus probably BUB-1 sumoylation (Figure 1H; Pelisch et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculated based on the requirement for GEI-17, an E3 SUMO-protein ligase

claim: The BHC module is recruited to kinetochores via the KNL-1 MELT repeats
source: These results show that the BHC module is recruited to kinetochores via the KNL-1 MELT repeats.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing BHC components fail to localize to kinetochores in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant

claim: During mitosis, CENP-F in mammals and HCP-1 in C. elegans are recruited to kinetochores through the BUB-1 kinase domain
source: During mitosis, CENP-F in mammals and HCP-1 in C. elegans, are recruited to kinetochores through the BUB-1 kinase domain (Edwards et al., 2018; Ciossani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2018 and Ciossani et al., 2018

claim: GFP-tagged HCP-1 localizes to kinetochores and ring domains in the presence of BUB-1FL but not BUB-1∆KD
source: GFP-tagged HCP-1 (and CLS-2) localized to kinetochores and ring domains in the presence of BUB-1FL, but not BUB-1∆KD (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2B

claim: CLS-2 localizes to kinetochores and ring domains in the presence of BUB-1FL but not BUB-1∆KD
source: GFP-tagged HCP-1 (and CLS-2) localized to kinetochores and ring domains in the presence of BUB-1FL, but not BUB-1∆KD (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2C

claim: HCP-1 is normally targeted to kinetochores and rings in the presence of kinase-dead BUB-1D814N mutant
source: Upon depletion of endogenous BUB-1 in the presence of the kinase-dead BUB-1D814N mutant, HCP-1 (and CLS-2) were normally targeted to kinetochores and rings (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2B

claim: CLS-2 is normally targeted to kinetochores and rings in the presence of kinase-dead BUB-1D814N mutant
source: Upon depletion of endogenous BUB-1 in the presence of the kinase-dead BUB-1D814N mutant, HCP-1 (and CLS-2) were normally targeted to kinetochores and rings (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2C

claim: BUB-1 recruits HCP-1 to kinetochores and rings through its kinase domain, but independently of kinase activity, in meiosis in C. elegans
source: Therefore, BUB-1 recruits HCP-1 (and CLS-2) to kinetochores and rings through its kinase domain, but independently of kinase activity, in meiosis in C. elegans.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing HCP-1 localization requires kinase domain but not kinase activity

claim: BUB-1 recruits CLS-2 to kinetochores and rings through its kinase domain, but independently of kinase activity, in meiosis in C. elegans
source: Therefore, BUB-1 recruits HCP-1 (and CLS-2) to kinetochores and rings through its kinase domain, but independently of kinase activity, in meiosis in C. elegans.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing CLS-2 localization requires kinase domain but not kinase activity

claim: Two main regions of HCP-1 (amino acid 111–340 and 1311–1386, referred to as CBD and KTD respectively) are essential for embryonic viability
source: Two main regions of HCP-1 (amino acid 111–340 and 1311–1386, hereafter referred to as CBD (CLS-2 Binding Domain) and KTD (Kinetochore Targeting Domain) respectively, see below), one at either terminus, were essential for embryonic viability (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), even though the mutant and wild-type transgenes were expressed at comparable levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by embryonic viability assays in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Deleting the KTD (HCP-1∆KTD), but not the CBD (HCP-1∆CBD), prevents kinetochore targeting of HCP-1
source: We found that deleting the KTD (HCP-1∆KTD), but not the CBD (HCP-1∆CBD), prevented kinetochore targeting of the corresponding deletion mutant HCP-1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2F

claim: The HCP-1 CBD truncation mutant prevents mCherry-fused CLS-2 kinetochore targeting
source: Accordingly, we found that the HCP-1 CBD truncation mutant prevented mCherry-fused CLS-2 kinetochore targeting (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: HCP-1 kinetochore targeting requires its KTD
source: Thus HCP-1 kinetochore targeting requires its KTD, while the HCP-1 CBD mediates CLS-2 kinetochore recruitment.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing HCP-1∆KTD fails to localize to kinetochores

claim: The HCP-1 CBD mediates CLS-2 kinetochore recruitment
source: Thus HCP-1 kinetochore targeting requires its KTD, while the HCP-1 CBD mediates CLS-2 kinetochore recruitment.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing HCP-1∆CBD prevents CLS-2 kinetochore targeting

claim: In most species, CLASPs targeting to their various subcellular localizations, including to kinetochores, relies on interactions with various adapter proteins via a C-terminal domain
source: In most species, CLASPs targeting to their various subcellular localizations, including to kinetochores, relies on interactions with various adapter proteins via a C-terminal domain (CTD; Akhmanova et al., 2001; Maiato et al., 2003; Hannak and Heald, 2006; Lansbergen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Akhmanova et al., 2001; Maiato et al., 2003; Hannak and Heald, 2006; Lansbergen et al., 2006

claim: CLS-2∆CTD does not target to the kinetochores during meiosis in oocytes or in mitosis in zygotes
source: In contrast to CLS-2FL, the CTD-deleted transgenic protein did not target to the kinetochores during meiosis in oocytes or in mitosis in zygotes (Figure 2H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), which is in line with previous findings on vertebrate CLASPs (Maiato et al., 2003).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, and supported by citation to Maiato et al., 2003

claim: The R970A mutated version of CLS-2 does not localize at kinetochores
source: Although this transgene was expressed at similar levels to the wild-type version (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), the R970A mutated protein did not localize at kinetochores, which confirmed the importance of this residue for the CLS-2 CTD function (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 2H and expression levels in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Both CLS-2FL and the CLS-2 CTD only, but not the R970A mutated version of the CTD, directly interact with HCP-1 CBD
source: We next performed a yeast two-hybrid-based assay between the CLS-2 CTD wild-type or R970A and the HCP-1 CBD, which confirmed that both CLS-2FL and the CLS-2 CTD only, but not the R970A mutated version of the CTD, directly interact with CLS-2 and likely mediate CLS-2 kinetochore targeting (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Shown by yeast two-hybrid assay in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: BHC module assembly in meiosis and mitosis requires the BUB-1 kinase domain and the HCP-1 KTD
source: Overall, our results show that BHC module assembly in meiosis and mitosis requires the BUB-1 kinase domain and the HCP-1 KTD, and involves HCP-1 CBD binding to the CLS-2 CTD through a conserved C-terminal VRK motif.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing requirements for these domains

claim: BHC module assembly involves HCP-1 CBD binding to the CLS-2 CTD through a conserved C-terminal VRK motif
source: Overall, our results show that BHC module assembly in meiosis and mitosis requires the BUB-1 kinase domain and the HCP-1 KTD, and involves HCP-1 CBD binding to the CLS-2 CTD through a conserved C-terminal VRK motif.
evidence: Concluded from yeast two-hybrid and localization experiments

claim: Depletion of endogenous KNL-1 in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes does not prevent assembly of bipolar spindles
source: Depletion of endogenous KNL-1 in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes did not prevent assembly of bipolar spindles, but the spindles were smaller and displayed a reduced microtubule density (Figure 3A and B), demonstrating that BHC module kinetochore targeting is essential for normal spindle assembly.
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B

claim: Spindles in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes are smaller and display reduced microtubule density
source: Depletion of endogenous KNL-1 in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes did not prevent assembly of bipolar spindles, but the spindles were smaller and displayed a reduced microtubule density (Figure 3A and B), demonstrating that BHC module kinetochore targeting is essential for normal spindle assembly.
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B

claim: BHC module kinetochore targeting is essential for normal spindle assembly
source: Depletion of endogenous KNL-1 in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes did not prevent assembly of bipolar spindles, but the spindles were smaller and displayed a reduced microtubule density (Figure 3A and B), demonstrating that BHC module kinetochore targeting is essential for normal spindle assembly.
evidence: Concluded from observation of smaller spindles with reduced microtubule density in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant

claim: KNL-1∆85-505 mutant spindles are capable of efficient chromosome segregation
source: These shorter KNL-1∆85-505 mutant spindles were however capable of efficient chromosome segregation, unlike spindles assembled in the complete absence of KNL-1 (Figure 3A–B, Video 1, Video 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A-B, Videos 1-2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Oocytes fully depleted of BUB-1 display severe spindle abnormalities and chromosome segregation defects
source: The KNL-1∆85-505 mutant spindles also contrasted with oocytes fully depleted of BUB-1, which displayed severe spindle abnormalities and chromosome segregation defects (Figure 3A, Video 1, Video 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A, Videos 1-2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: GEI-17-depleted oocytes with endogenous wildtype KNL-1 form normal bipolar spindles and chromosome segregation is accurate
source: Yet in the presence of endogenous wildtype KNL-1, GEI-17-depleted oocytes formed normal bipolar spindles and chromosome segregation was accurate (Figure 3A, Video 2).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A and Video 2

claim: The kinetochore and ring domain pools of BHC module act redundantly for spindle assembly and chromosome segregation in oocytes
source: We thus hypothesized that the kinetochore and ring domain pools of BHC module could act redundantly for spindle assembly and chromosome segregation in oocytes.
evidence: Hypothesized based on observations that depleting either pool alone has milder phenotypes than depleting both

claim: The mild spindle phenotype observed in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes is strongly aggravated upon simultaneous depletion of KNL-1 and GEI-17
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the mild spindle phenotypes observed in the absence of BHC module localization at kinetochores was strongly aggravated upon simultaneous BHC delocalization at ring domains after simultaneous depletion of KNL-1 and GEI-17 in KNL-1∆85-505 mutant oocytes (Figure 3A–B, Video 2).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 3A-B and Video 2

claim: Functions of kinetochore and ring domain pools of the BHC module are partially redundant in the control of spindle assembly and chromosome segregation
source: Therefore, functions of kinetochore and ring domain pools of the BHC module are partially redundant in the control of spindle assembly and chromosome segregation.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that depleting both pools has more severe phenotypes than depleting either alone

claim: CLS-2 is primarily acting at the chromosomes and not as a diffuse pool of protein along the spindle
source: This finding also implies that CLS-2 is primarily acting at the chromosomes and not as a diffuse pool of protein along the spindle.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that kinetochore and ring domain localization are important for CLS-2 function

claim: During mitosis in C. elegans, HCP-1/2 have been proposed to primarily act as CLS-2 kinetochore-targeting proteins
source: During mitosis in C. elegans, HCP-1/2 have been proposed to primarily act as CLS-2 kinetochore-targeting proteins (Cheeseman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheeseman et al., 2005

claim: Spindle assembly is severely disrupted in BUB-1∆KD, HCP-1∆KTD, and HCP-1∆CBD mutants with an apolar spindle phenotype and reduced microtubule density
source: Spindle assembly was severely disrupted in all mutants with an apolar spindle phenotype and reduced microtubule density. Meiotic chromosome segregation occurred, although lagging chromosomes during anaphase and retracted polar bodies during telophase were evident (Figure 4B–C, Video 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 4B-C, Video 3, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Mitotic chromosome segregation is strongly perturbed in the HCP-1∆CBD or HCP-1∆KTD mutants in absence of endogenous HCP-1/2 proteins, with evident sister chromatid co-segregation
source: Mitotic chromosome segregation was also strongly perturbed in the HCP-1∆CBD or HCP-1∆KTD mutants in absence of endogenous HCP-1/2 proteins, with evident sister chromatid co-segregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Expression of BUB-1∆KD, HCP-1∆CBD, or HCP-1∆KTD following depletion and/or deletion of BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 recapitulates the bub-1(RNAi) and hcp-1/2(RNAi) phenotypes
source: Thus, expression of BUB-1∆KD, HCP-1∆CBD, or HCP-1∆KTD following depletion and/or deletion of BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 recapitulated the bub-1(RNAi) and hcp-1/2(RNAi) phenotypes, with disorganized spindles and chromosome segregation defects.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of phenotypes across different mutants

claim: The primary function of BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 occurs in the context of the BHC module
source: Overall, these results suggest that the primary function of BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 occurs in the context of the BHC module.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing that disrupting BHC module integrity causes severe phenotypes

claim: CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 localizes to kinetochores and to ring domains
source: We first verified that CLS-2 fused to GFP and to HCP-11154-1386 localized to kinetochores and to ring domains (Figure 4E), compared to GFP-tagged wild-type CLS2.
evidence: Shown by imaging in Figure 4E

claim: CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 can sustain embryonic development and viability in absence of endogenous CLS-2
source: Next to ensure that CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 was functional, we checked that it could sustain embryonic development and viability in absence of endogenous CLS-2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Shown by embryonic viability assay in Figure 4F

claim: CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 supports normal meiotic and mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation upon cls-2(RNAi) in oocytes
source: Accordingly, CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 also supported normal meiotic and mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation upon cls-2(RNAi) in oocytes (Figure 4G, Video 4).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 4G and Video 4

claim: The HCP-1 KTD is both necessary and sufficient for localization
source: CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 also localized normally in absence of HCP-1 (Figure 4E), which suggests that the HCP-1 KTD is both necessary and sufficient for localization.
evidence: Inferred from observation that CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386 localizes normally without endogenous HCP-1

claim: Spindles and chromosome segregation in oocytes and zygotes are severely affected upon hcp-1(RNAi) in the presence of CLS-2::GFP::HCP-11154-1386
source: However, spindles and chromosome segregation in oocytes and zygotes were severely affected upon hcp-1(RNAi) (Figure 4G).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 4G

claim: HCP-1/2 do not act only as targeting proteins for CLS-2 and likely have other roles in regulating microtubule dynamics in oocytes
source: Embryonic viability was also low in this condition (Figure 4F), suggesting that HCP-1/2 do not act only as targeting proteins for CLS-2 and likely have other roles in regulating microtubule dynamics in oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from observation that targeting CLS-2 to kinetochores independently of HCP-1/2 is not sufficient to rescue phenotypes

claim: BHC module integrity and proper localization is essential for meiotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation in oocytes
source: Overall, these results show that BHC module integrity and proper localization is essential for meiotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation in oocytes.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing that disrupting BHC module integrity or localization causes severe phenotypes

claim: In human CLASP2, TOGL2 is essential for microtubule catastrophe suppression, whereas TOGL3 enhances rescue
source: In human CLASP2, these domains have specific functions. TOGL2 is essential for microtubule catastrophe suppression, whereas TOGL3 enhances rescue (Lawrence et al., 2018; Aher et al., 2018; Girão et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawrence et al., 2018; Aher et al., 2018; Girão et al., 2020

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of CLASPs can inhibit TOGL functions in human CLASP2
source: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of CLASPs, responsible for kinetochore targeting, can inhibit these functions in human CLASP2, while the TOGL1 is required to release this auto-inhibition (Aher et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aher et al., 2018

claim: The TOGL1 is required to release auto-inhibition by the CTD in human CLASP2
source: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of CLASPs, responsible for kinetochore targeting, can inhibit these functions in human CLASP2, while the TOGL1 is required to release this auto-inhibition (Aher et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aher et al., 2018

claim: A conserved Serine/Arginine-rich (S/R-rich) region, important for microtubule lattice binding through electrostatic interactions, separates TOGL2 and 3
source: Additionally, a conserved Serine/Arginine-rich (S/R-rich) region, important for microtubule lattice binding through electrostatic interactions, separates TOGL2 and 3 (Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2012

claim: CLS-2 contains only two TOGL domains (TOGL2 and 3) separated by an S/R-rich region
source: Sequence analysis showed that CLS-2 contains only two TOGL domains (TOGL2 and 3) separated by an S/R-rich region, and a CTD separated from TOGL3 by a linker region predicted to be largely unfolded and a small also unfolded C-terminal tail (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Determined by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Five CLS-2 mutants (CLS-2∆TOGL2, CLS-2TOGL2-WKR/A, CLS-2∆SR-rich, CLS-2∆CTD, CLS-2R970A) are unable to sustain embryonic viability in absence of endogenous CLS-2
source: All transgenes were expressed at comparable levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), but only five mutants were unable to sustain embryonic viability in absence of endogenous CLS-2. These corresponded to deletion or point mutations within TOGL2 (CLS-2∆TOGL2, CLS-2TOGL2-WKR/A), the S/R-rich region (CLS-2∆SR-rich), and the CTD (CLS-2∆CTD, CLS-2R970A) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown by embryonic viability assay in Figure 5B and expression levels in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Deleting TOGL3, or the linker region between TOGL3 and the CTD, or the C-terminal tail has no significant effect on embryonic viability upon depletion of endogenous CLS-2
source: In contrast, deleting TOGL3, or the linker region between TOGL3 and the CTD, or the C-terminal tail had no significant effect on embryonic viability upon depletion of endogenous CLS-2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown by embryonic viability assay in Figure 5B

claim: TOGL3 lacks several conserved amino-acids present in TOGL2 that normally contribute to microtubule binding in human CLASPs and to tubulin binding in XMAP215 family proteins
source: Sequence analysis revealed that TOGL3 lacks several conserved amino-acids (present in TOGL2 and mutated in the CLS-2TOGL2-WKR/A mutant, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) corresponding to residues that normally contribute to microtubule binding in human CLASPs and to tubulin binding in XMAP215 family proteins (Leano et al., 2013; Funk et al., 2014).
evidence: Determined by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and supported by citations to Leano et al., 2013; Funk et al., 2014

claim: Mutating or deleting TOGL2, the S/R-rich region or the CTD leads to phenotypes comparable to the full loss of function of CLS-2 with severely disorganized spindles, inaccurate chromosome segregation and polar body extrusion failures
source: We confirmed a loss-of-function phenotype by analyzing meiotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation in oocytes lacking endogenous CLS-2. Mutating or deleting TOGL2, the S/R-rich region or the CTD led to phenotypes comparable to the full loss of function of CLS-2 with severely disorganized spindles, inaccurate chromosome segregation and polar body extrusion failures (Figure 5D, Video 6).
evidence: Shown by live imaging in Figure 5D and Video 6

claim: As in human CLASP2, CLS-2 functions via a single TOGL domain (TOGL2)
source: Thus, as in human CLASP2, CLS-2 functions via a single TOGL domain (TOGL2), and also requires the CTD for HCP-1 binding and the S/R-rich region for potential microtubule lattice-interaction.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing TOGL2 is essential while TOGL3 is not

claim: CLS-2 requires the CTD for HCP-1 binding
source: Thus, as in human CLASP2, CLS-2 functions via a single TOGL domain (TOGL2), and also requires the CTD for HCP-1 binding and the S/R-rich region for potential microtubule lattice-interaction.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing CTD is required for kinetochore localization and HCP-1 interaction

claim: CLS-2 requires the S/R-rich region for potential microtubule lattice-interaction
source: Thus, as in human CLASP2, CLS-2 functions via a single TOGL domain (TOGL2), and also requires the CTD for HCP-1 binding and the S/R-rich region for potential microtubule lattice-interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of S/R-rich region for function and known role of S/R-rich regions in microtubule binding

claim: 100 nM BUB-1 does not display any strong effect on the microtubule growth rate, on catastrophe and rescue frequencies, nor on the time spent in pause by microtubules
source: Consistent with BUB-1 not being a microtubule-associated protein (MAP), analysis of microtubule dynamics showed that 100 nM BUB-1 did not display any strong effect on the microtubule growth rate, on catastrophe and rescue frequencies, nor on the time spent in pause by microtubules (Figure 6B–F, Video 7).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays in Figure 6B-F and Video 7

claim: BUB-1 on its own does not interact with microtubules in a pelleting assay
source: BUB-1 on its own also did not interact with microtubules in a pelleting assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), nor show any microtubule-bundling activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: Shown by microtubule pelleting assay in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: BUB-1 does not show any microtubule-bundling activity
source: BUB-1 on its own also did not interact with microtubules in a pelleting assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), nor show any microtubule-bundling activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: Shown by microtubule bundling assay in Figure 6G

claim: Both HCP-1 and CLS-2-GFP independently display strong microtubule-bundling activity
source: In contrast, both HCP-1 and CLS-2-GFP independently displayed strong microtubule-bundling activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: Shown by microtubule bundling assay in Figure 6G

claim: 100 nM HCP-1 has a mild but significant promoting effect on the microtubule growth rate (1.4-fold increase)
source: Consistent with a previous study showing that human CENP-F can stimulate microtubule polymerization in vitro Feng et al., 2006, 100 nM HCP-1 had a mild but significant promoting effect on the microtubule growth rate (1.4-fold increase).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays and supported by citation to Feng et al., 2006

claim: The promoting effect of HCP-1 on microtubule growth rate is abrogated by addition of 100 nM BUB-1
source: This was interestingly abrogated by addition of 100 nM BUB-1, but not by a combination of BUB-1 and CLS-2-GFP (100 nM each; Figure 6B–F, Video 7).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays in Figure 6B-F and Video 7

claim: 100 nM CLS-2-GFP alone inhibits the microtubule growth rate (1.1-fold reduction)
source: In contrast, 100 nM CLS-2-GFP alone had the opposite effect and inhibited the microtubule growth rate (1.1-fold reduction), which is consistent with the effect of human or Drosophila CLASPs on microtubule dynamics (Yu et al., 2016; Moriwaki and Goshima, 2016; Aher et al., 2018).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays and supported by citations to Yu et al., 2016; Moriwaki and Goshima, 2016; Aher et al., 2018

claim: CLS-2-GFP has significant catastrophe-suppressing, and rescue- and pause-promoting activities
source: Also consistent with previous reports on CLASPs, we found that CLS-2-GFP had significant catastrophe-suppressing, and rescue- and pause-promoting activities (Figure 6B–F, Video 7; Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Lawrence et al., 2018; Aher et al., 2018).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays in Figure 6B-F and Video 7, and supported by citations to Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Lawrence et al., 2018; Aher et al., 2018

claim: CLS-2 is unlikely to function as a microtubule polymerase, as neither of the two TOGL domains interacted with free tubulin
source: Furthermore, and like human CLASPs, CLS-2 is unlikely to function as a microtubule polymerase, as neither of the two TOGL domains interacted with free tubulin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Aher et al., 2018).
evidence: Shown by gel filtration assay in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and supported by citation to Aher et al., 2018

claim: The effect of CLS-2-GFP on catastrophe is independent of HCP-1 and/or BUB-1
source: The effect of CLS-2-GFP on catastrophe was independent of HCP-1 and/or BUB-1 (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays in Figure 6C-F

claim: The rescue-promoting effect of CLS-2-GFP is increased by addition of HCP-1 alone (twofold increase), but not by a combination of HCP-1 and BUB-1
source: This is in contrast to its effect on rescue promotion, which was increased by addition of HCP-1 alone (twofold increase), but not by a combination of HCP-1 and BUB-1.
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays

claim: Reconstituting the full BHC module (BUB-1, HCP-1, and CLS-2-GFP together) in vitro results in a strong increase in the pause-promoting activity (21-fold increase in the time spent in pause) compared to all other conditions tested
source: The most surprising effect of reconstituting the full BHC module (BUB-1, HCP-1, and CLS-2-GFP together) in vitro was the strong increase in the pause-promoting activity (21-fold increase in the time spent in pause) compared to all other conditions tested (Figure 6F, Video 7).
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays in Figure 6F and Video 7

claim: Reconstituting the BHC module in vitro displays both additive and synergistic effects on microtubule dynamics compared to individual components
source: Thus, reconstituting the BHC module in vitro displays both additive (promotion of the growth rate and rescue frequency by HCP-1 and CLS-2 respectively, and inhibition of catastrophe by CLS-2) and synergistic (promotion of pause) effects on microtubule dynamics compared to individual components, which leads to microtubule stabilization.
evidence: Concluded from TIRF microscopy assays showing different effects of individual components versus the full module

claim: BUB-1 and HCP-1 can modulate the effect of CLS-2 on microtubule dynamics
source: This also indicates that BUB-1 and HCP-1 can modulate the effect of CLS-2 on microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from observations that effects of CLS-2 differ when combined with BUB-1 and/or HCP-1

claim: CLS-2R970A-GFP alone has identical effects on all microtubule dynamics parameters tested, as compared to wild-type CLS-2-GFP
source: Importantly, this mutant alone had identical effects on all microtubule dynamics parameters tested, as compared to wild-type CLS-2-GFP, suggesting that CLS-2R970A-GFP was functional.
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays

claim: CLS-2R970A-GFP does not display the same increase of microtubule pausing when combined with HCP-1 and BUB-1
source: However, it did not display the same increase of microtubule pausing when combined with HCP-1 and BUB-1, showing that this synergistic effect specifically required formation of an intact BHC module.
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy assays

claim: The synergistic pause-promoting effect specifically requires formation of an intact BHC module
source: However, it did not display the same increase of microtubule pausing when combined with HCP-1 and BUB-1, showing that this synergistic effect specifically required formation of an intact BHC module.
evidence: Concluded from observation that CLS-2R970A-GFP, which cannot bind HCP-1, does not show increased pausing with BUB-1 and HCP-1

claim: BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 in the context of an intact BHC module are important contributors in the regulation of microtubule dynamics
source: Overall, our in vitro results are consistent with our in vivo data and suggest BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 in the context of an intact BHC module are important contributors in the regulation of microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Concluded from in vitro TIRF microscopy assays showing synergistic effects of the full BHC module

claim: In C. elegans, binding to HCP-1 and BUB-1 can modulate CLS-2 effect on microtubules
source: Overall, we showed here that, in C. elegans, binding to HCP-1 and BUB-1 could modulate CLS-2 effect on microtubules.
evidence: Concluded from in vitro experiments showing different effects of CLS-2 alone versus in complex with HCP-1 and BUB-1

claim: BubR1 and Bub1 are clear paralogous proteins
source: As BubR1 and Bub1 are clear paralogous proteins, and CENP-E and CENP-F have been proposed to be distantly related paralogs, it would be interesting to determine if similar synergistic regulation of microtubule dynamics exists between BubR1, CENP-E and CLASP proteins in vertebrates (Ciossani et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Ciossani et al., 2018

claim: CENP-E and CENP-F have been proposed to be distantly related paralogs
source: As BubR1 and Bub1 are clear paralogous proteins, and CENP-E and CENP-F have been proposed to be distantly related paralogs, it would be interesting to determine if similar synergistic regulation of microtubule dynamics exists between BubR1, CENP-E and CLASP proteins in vertebrates (Ciossani et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a proposal and supported by citation to Ciossani et al., 2018

claim: Interaction between spindle microtubules and kinetochores is central to the bi-orientation of chromosomes
source: During cell division, chromosome segregation is orchestrated by a microtubule-based spindle. Interaction between spindle microtubules and kinetochores is central to the bi-orientation of chromosomes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Microtubules are initially dynamic to allow spindle assembly and kinetochore attachments, which is essential for chromosome alignment
source: Initially dynamic to allow spindle assembly and kinetochore attachments, which is essential for chromosome alignment, microtubules are eventually stabilized for efficient segregation of sister chromatids and homologous chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis I, respectively.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Microtubules are eventually stabilized for efficient segregation of sister chromatids and homologous chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis I
source: Initially dynamic to allow spindle assembly and kinetochore attachments, which is essential for chromosome alignment, microtubules are eventually stabilized for efficient segregation of sister chromatids and homologous chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis I, respectively.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: BHC components stabilize microtubules, which is essential for meiotic spindle formation and accurate chromosome segregation
source: Using a combination of in vivo structure-function analyses of BHC components and in vitro microtubule-based assays, we show that BHC components stabilize microtubules, which is essential for meiotic spindle formation and accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: Concluded from combination of in vivo and in vitro experiments

claim: BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 synergistically control kinetochore-microtubule dynamics by promoting microtubule pause
source: Overall, our results show that BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 do not only act as targeting components for CLS-2 at kinetochores, but also synergistically control kinetochore-microtubule dynamics by promoting microtubule pause.
evidence: Concluded from in vitro experiments showing synergistic pause promotion by the full BHC module

claim: BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 actively participate in the control of kinetochore-microtubule dynamics in the context of an intact BHC module to promote spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation in meiosis
source: Together, our results suggest that BUB-1 and HCP-1/2 actively participate in the control of kinetochore-microtubule dynamics in the context of an intact BHC module to promote spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation in meiosis.
evidence: Concluded from combination of in vivo and in vitro experiments
